full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a little bit about what we’re doing, which is basically interviewing people, women engineering students across all different disciplines to find out, how are they going on placements and why are they going on placements and a bit about why they wanted to do engineering and their engineering experiences, so far. And we’re looking – to compare that with what it’s like when they’re in the industry (right) to get some idea of what women expect from the industry and whether the industry meets their expectations and we’re aiming to increase the retention of women in the industry (right) which is basically what we’re looking at. So if I start off asking you just a few background information questions - what course is it that you’re on?

Subject:	Civil engineering.

Interviewer:	You’re doing civil engineering and is it the Master’s or the…?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you going on a placement?

Subject:	It’s – I’m undecided at the moment. I’ve got a sponsor (right) and it’s all just up in the air at the moment about whether I’m going to go or whether I’m going to stay (OK) I’m not quite certain yet.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did erm double maths, physics and economics.

Interviewer:	Right, OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, I went to a private secondary school and a state sixth form.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. Have you got any work experience?

Subject:	Not in engineering, no.

Interviewer:	OK, are either of your parents engineers? What do they do?

Subject:	No. My mum is something in accounts – she’s not an accountant but she does something in accounts (yeah) and my dad, he’s retired now but he was a university administrator.

Interviewer:	OK, so we’re going to talk about why you wanted to do engineering in the first place. So why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

Subject:	Erm, it was basically that I was doing maths and physics at A level, and I was trying to find a degree that would have substantial proportions of that in it (yeah) and basically my physics teacher at A level was really good and I went spoke to him and said, look, these are the bits I’ve enjoyed, what do you suggest? And he suggested civil engineering and I looked into it a bit more and just…

Interviewer:	Why then did you do maths and physics A levels and not…?

Subject:	They were just the subjects that at GCSE I enjoyed – I was good at, and I knew I could cope with doing them at a higher level. There were other GCSE subjects that I might have enjoyed but I couldn’t see myself actually managing to complete an A level course. (yes) So, it was a combination of being good and enjoying it.

Interviewer:	OK, what about your family – were they supportive of your choices?

Subject:	Yes, they – it’s always – not been expected, but always been a highly favourable option, to go off to university and do something, like, both my older sisters did and yeah, I think.

Interviewer:	But the subject wasn’t really an issue?

Subject:	No, but I mean – I did a lot of sport when I was younger and it was – basically it was not told to me, but made sound, like, don’t do sports. So, I wasn’t really allowed to do a sport one but anything else, they were fine.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do any career research and did you know any – any other engineers to talk to, to speak to – what it was like?

Subject:	Not really, basically, I knew that having an engineering degree wouldn’t – didn’t just lead you to doing engineering. When, I knew that if I came out with an engineering degree, I could go off and do all sorts of stuff. So to me, the fact of getting a degree was more important than the necessary career afterwards.

Interviewer:	OK, what does appeal to you about engineering?

Subject:	Um, I guess it has its logic and the mathematical bits, where in a lot of other subjects you can write an essay or write something out and it won’t necessarily have a right answer (yeah) whereas in engineering quite often, well most of the time, you work something out, you’ll come to an answer and it’s either right or wrong (yes) and I just – I like that.

Interviewer:	OK. Is there anything in particular that attracted you to civil engineering rather than say mechanical or electrical engineering?

Subject:	Civil engineering just sounded more practical to me, and like it made more sense to me, so having something – and I’ve found in some modules its not quite this way, but having something you can visualise and something big like a building, you can really see it’s there, whereas things like mechanical – it all gets a bit technical.

Interviewer:	Did you look into other subjects?

Subject:	I didn’t – I think I dismissed them quite quickly just as a kind of oh, I don’t think I’ll enjoy that bit – right, what’s next? And I came across civil and thought I’d enjoy that.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to study at [this] University?

Subject:	Erm, it was - sport was a big pull for me and I’d had a couple of friends who’d been at [this university] – they’d had a really, really good time and I mean, in some ways, it was an added bonus that the civil engineering department happened to be really good, but it was mainly just for the sport.

Interviewer:	OK, did you say that you’re sponsored?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to do that?

Subject:	It was – they’ve got, in the civil engineering department, they’ve got a group of companies where you submit a general application form for sponsorship. It goes out to all those companies and then it’s – basically I didn’t see any reason not to.

Interviewer:	Was that after you’d started at University?

Subject:	It was a couple of months into the first year and the department said oh, here’s the application forms – if you can fill ‘em out, fill ‘em out and give ‘em back to us and it just made sense.

Interviewer:	So, the indecision about the sandwich bit at the minute, is that your choice or the company?

Subject:	That’s complicated. Er, actually in May last year, I had a baby and so it’s a case of whether I can find a job for a placement year which will allow me to still look after her because I know that if I went onto a site, I’d be expected to be on site for stupid long hours and I wouldn’t be able to look after my daughter. So it’s mostly just that if they can – if my sponsors can offer me a job where I can either be in an office, where I work regular hours, hopefully, live at home so I’ve got a support network, then I’m going into industry. If not – if they can’t offer me that then I’ll stay – just go straight on through. But that – that should be decided in the next couple of weeks.

Interviewer:	What appeals to you about doing the sandwich course?

Subject:	It’s mostly to help me have an idea of whether I actually want to go off and work in er the industry when I graduate, or whether I realise, during the year in industry, that actually it’s not for me. I’d rather realise that in one year out, than apply for a job, get a job and then realise after I’ve graduated, that actually it’s not for me. So it’s just to help me make my mind up.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise it was so male-dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, I knew it was quite highly male dominated, because when we went on open days around the country, like the students who’d show you round the university, from the department, would say oh yeah, there’s only 2 girls in my year and so you get to know pretty quickly. So in my maths classes and physics classes at A level, so they were male dominated and you just realise that – it’s not something that huge numbers of girls actually want to go into. So, yeah.

Interviewer:	Did that ever concern you?

Subject:	No, not really, it didn’t really bother me. I mean the only – I knew that the industry was largely male dominated, and in some ways, applying to university, I thought that actually it might play in my favour, because applying as a girl, they’re trying to get girls in engineering, therefore, if on paper me and another candidate were exactly equal, the fact that I was a girl would then, perhaps – I don’t know, go in my favour and help me get on….

Interviewer:	Do you think that’ll work the same in the workplace, as well?

Subject:	I’m not sure because as far as the sponsorship interviews went, I got a few interviews and one in particular I went to, and another girl off my course got interviewed and she’d – both of us found that the man who was interviewing was just – didn’t want to know (right). And we almost felt like saying why did you give us an interview – if you quite blatantly – he was – I think it was partly that he just couldn’t communicate with girls, and he just found it really hard to interview us, whereas one of the guys who went for an interview, with the same man, said that they got on great, were chatting the whole way through. So that’s when you start to realise that actually it’s not a problem with the girls it’s some – I think it’s the kind of older generation of people in the industry at the moment, just struggle to see or struggle to cope with having women coming into the industry, but I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

Subject:	I don’t – I’ve thought about that one quite a lot, because in some ways there’s always gonna be a finite number of girls who actually want to do a science based erm projects, and for some reason or another and I don’t know what the reason is, it’s a lower number than guys. Erm, so in some ways, encouraging girls to go into engineering might – it might get more girls doing a degree but I think the end results might not be more women going into the actual industry. It’s like I’m doing a degree but I’m not certain at the moment whether I actually want to go off and be in engineering or whether I want to go and do something else. So – er, it’s worth encouraging because there’s – there are some girls who may think, oh no, I can’t do that, boys do that. So it might get a few of them, but I don’t know how effective it would actually be.

Interviewer:	Do you think that if people aren’t so much actually encouraged into the industry that they might need to be better informed about the industry because they’ve got to make that decision? When I did A levels, I didn’t know anything about engineering so I would never even have considered it.

Subject:	Yes, that might be worth – yeah, so you would catch people who had never even considered it, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what if anything would have encouraged or discouraged you from doing engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I don’t think – the only things that would have altered my decision, would be either my ability at the subject or my liking for it. I don’t think it has anything to do with anything on the outside of the pure subject. If there’s – I don’t really know. If there’d been more of the parts of the physics and maths that I hadn’t enjoyed, then I probably wouldn’t have done it, but because it’s full of the bits that I was good at and enjoyed, then other things really didn’t come into play that much.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think ability at the subject’s got to be a foremost thing and man-management – just being able to communicate with the team, work in a team, erm, I don’t know, I guess that – I’d probably find that easier to answer if I’d actually gone out into the industry.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any things about engineers that you would describe as male characteristics or female characteristics?

Subject:	I think, even on the face of it, it’s very much the individuals that actually end up doing engineering. The girls, particularly on my course, I would say equal ability as the guys but if you take a girl from another area, who hadn’t gone into engineering, then she wouldn’t necessarily have all the qualities that she’d need. But I think, from what I’ve seen, the girls who end up doing the course I’m doing, have the attributes you need – that that’s because they’re the kind of people that will choose to do engineering.

Interviewer:	OK, you’ve said that you think there may be some advantages to being a woman – do you think there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	I’d say it’s only just coming up against people in the industry who – they don’t necessarily not want women in the erm industry, but find it easier to get on with men, who apply for the job. Erm, I guess that’s one of the disadvantages. And, from personal experience, I can see how, if a woman wanted to balance family and like for example working in construction, they’d find that very difficult. I guess that’s – nowadays that’s not a disadvantage that’s purely tied to a woman. It’s just a choice that they have to make.

Interviewer:	OK, when you started on your course here, what did you expect from your degree programme?

Subject:	I don’t really know.

Interviewer:	Is it what you expected in terms of like things you’ve been taught, the types of skills and gender proportions?

Subject:	Yeah. I mean the gender proportions actually when I arrived, there were more girls than I thought there were going to be.

Interviewer:	Was there?

Subject:	So I think, out of the arranged courses – there were like 28, there were 5 girls, which to me, arriving at that, seemed quite a large number. As far as what we’ve been taught, I knew that it was going to be a mix, between practical modules and management modules and that’s what’s come out of it. Some of the practical ones I didn’t foresee as us actually doing, like very much the hydraulics and fluids ones, I hadn’t really expected that so much and I think that’s shown ‘cos those are the ones I struggled more with. Those are the bits of physics I’m not very good with. But apart from that, no, it’s pretty much as I expected.

Interviewer:	What do you think have been the best and the worst things about your course, so far?

Subject:	Er, the best is, for me, coming into course without much knowledge about the whole industry, I knew the general – the general aspects, but probably just finding out more about the industry and learning about it as you, as you progress. The worst things – I don’t actually - I don’t think there are any particular aspects that I would stand like and say, oh no those have been awful.

Interviewer:	Is there any aspects that if you were to design the course, anything that you would change?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t think so.

Interviewer:	That’s ok. Have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, yes, we’ve had one female lecturer. She’s been in the management side of it. (right) But that’s – we had one module in the first year, which was partly taught by her and a module this year, that’s been partly taught by her. Apart from that, they’re all male.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any differences in the styles of teaching between male and female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, I think male lecturers are a lot more – well, in general, you’ve still got exceptions, but they’re generally a lot more direct, whereas I don’t know whether it’s because of the type of module that she’s teaching – the female lecturer is more wafflely as it were (yeah) using more words and less of the mathematical and practical applications.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that male lecturers treat the female students differently to the males?

Subject:	Well some of them, very particularly, you see they struggle with – they’re quite happy to sit and chat to the guys but then find it very hard to – they don’t really know what to say and it’s almost as if you’re – you’re not somebody who’s normal. Er, I mean there are extreme sides of it, there’s one lecturer who – yeah – completely could not hold down a conversation with a girl if he tried, but then with other ones who’ll quite happily chat to both equally, so it’s down to individuals.

Interviewer:	What about the female lecturer, did she treat all the students the same?

Subject:	Yeah, pretty much – I think so. I think it’s very interesting the way the guys on the course treat her, which perhaps makes it more difficult for her to chat to them. It’s – she’s my personal tutor so, so she knows me better anyway. So it’s quite difficult to see how she treats the other female students and the other male ones.

Interviewer:	OK, yeah – I was going to ask you about personal tutors as well – are you pleased that you’ve got a female personal tutor?

Subject:	I’m pleased that I’ve got the personal tutor I have – particularly last year, when I was going through all the having a baby stuff, she was – she was quite good at that and I can see how some of the male personal tutors just wouldn’t have really known what to do. So I’m quite glad to have her, but I could see how actually some of the male personal tutors would have been perfectly good at it, but at the end of the day er I was quite glad to have her.

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the greatest influence on you, since you started your degree?

Subject:	I don’t – I don’t really know. I don’t think there has been one particular driving influence to make me – I don’t know – want to carry on and do work. It’s just – it’s a degree, its all I want at the end of the day. Well, it’s the main thing I want so I don’t think there’s been any particular influence.

Interviewer:	Did you ever think about giving up last year then?

Subject:	No, I did think about the possibility of taking a year out but then I realised that I’d then just have a year when I was doing nothing much, erm, and at the end of the day if I’d dropped out last year, I’d have no degree, I’d have debt and basically I wouldn’t have anywhere to go. Whereas, if I stayed in University, yes, I’ll have debt by the end of it, but I’ll have a degree and actually I think I get to see my daughter a lot more being a student than I would having a proper job in the real world. So, to me, it was never particularly an option to drop out.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s made you more determined in some ways?

Subject:	Yeah, I think, because I know I have to – I really have to get this degree. I have to pass it. Whereas, before, yeah I wanted to but it wasn’t such a necessary importance – whereas now, yeah, if I – if I drop out at any point, then I’ve basically got nothing and I’ve got my daughter to support and I’ve got no way of supporting her (yeah) so everything’s a lot – well, in some ways everything’s a lot easier if I just carry on through and actually get the degree.

Interviewer:	OK, did the type of teaching that you’ve experienced, involve much interaction with students? Like, do you have to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s quite a lot of the course work’s are based in a group of – of I think the biggest group’s been 6 and then all the way down to just working in pairs.

Interviewer:	Do you generally get to choose who you work with?

Subject:	Erm, last year it was mostly we were put in groups, because, obviously, you arrive at Uni and of course you don’t know anybody and it’d be difficult to – for everybody to find groups. So last year they very much put you in groups. Er, I’m sure it was done alphabetically, it was normally the same people but this year it’s much more go away, find your group (yeah), come back, tell us your group and so yeah, this year we’ve got to choose more.

Interviewer:	In that situation how do you decide who you work with?

Subject:	Oh largely, people just end up working with their friends. People go with who they got on with anyway and it just makes it all a lot more simpler about trying to meet up. The – by the time we got towards the end of last year, where you were with a group of people that you just didn’t really know, didn’t get – well, didn’t not get on with, but didn’t get on with particularly well – and it is a lot easier to work in a group where it’s your friends.

Interviewer:	Do you think that males or females are easier to work with, or is that down to individuals?

Subject:	I think it’s just down to individuals. I’m just trying to think – I’ve worked in a few groups with one other girl in, but apart from that it’s – I’ve been working as the only girl in the group, and…

Interviewer:	Do you prefer that?

Subject:	I don’t really mind. Erm, I don’t think it made much difference. I don’t know whether it was the particular girl that I was working with, but it didn’t really make much difference whether it was entirely a group of guys and me, or a couple of guys with me and her (yeah). So, it didn’t end up making much difference.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, there was a bit of a bad exp – well, not a bad experience, but last year when they were starting to mix the groups between courses – so you’d have MENG people, BENG people and ANDN and you’d end up with all – all the ranges of abilities and levels of commitment and that was quite hard trying to get – and it ends up that I think one of the guys, who was in my group for that has – he’s since left, but I think he failed last year and it was very hard getting somebody who had a much lower level of commitment to the course, to – to work effectively in the group (Yeah). You were running around after them, hassling them to do some work but apart from that things have all just gone on quite nicely. The only problem comes when one person doesn’t do the work.

Interviewer:	Yeah. What aspects of university teaching or advice, do you think will help you if you go on placement?

Subject:	Er, very practical based modules, like the surveying modules where you actually go out and learn how to use the instruments. I think that would be invaluable. It would be – you wouldn’t want to go onto site without that. Erm, I think the group work probably does help, in that aspect, because at least you’ve had experience before working on engineer based erm projects with a range of people and a range of skills, I guess those two things will help.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any skills you’ve acquired from previous work experience might be useful on your placement?

Subject:	Er, just working as a team, will be the only particular one from the jobs that I’ve had. Erm, being able to interact with a range or group of people who work effectively as a team.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement at the moment – this stage in the course?

Subject:	I think it all depends on what job I got sent out to do. Er, I would be extremely nervous and feel slightly under prepared because a lot of people who will be going on their industrial placement worked last summer in industry, so they’ve got 3 months or whatever of experience, and I haven’t got that. I’ve never actually been onto a site but I can’t see myself ending up in a job, next year, if I do go into industry next year, that will require me to go on site all the time. I think it would be more that if I do take a placement year then it will be a placement in an office er I don’t really know what doing – design work or something like that.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the university could do anything to help students prepare more for the workplace?

Subject:	There is CIVSOC, which they organise site visits and that would be very useful. Unfortunately, they go on those site visits on Wednesdays, which is when sport is, so I can’t go on those site visits. Erm, I don’t – I think the department’s set up quite well, apart from that, just to help you. There’s all sorts of people who’ve got practical experience, who you can go and talk to if you want to, er so the only thing to do to help more is to tell CIVSOC to do their visits another time.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the educational experience and the way you’re taught, reflects the reality of what it’s like in the workplace?

Subject:	Not hugely. I mean there’s a lot of stuff we’re doing now, like you’re sitting in a lecture hall, you’re writing notes and you can see how the stuff you’re being taught will help you but the – the day to day, what we do, I don’t think it’s anything like what you’d actually be doing in a job.

Interviewer:	Do you think it should be geared more than it is, or do you think that they’re two separate things?

Subject:	I think it’s good the way it is, because if you want to get practical experience you can go off and you can get a job in your holidays or in your year out. I think that’s when you’ll find out about working on a site and all that stuff. So I think it’s – they don’t need to have any more of the practical side of it, actually on the course.

Interviewer:	OK, with respect to the organisation that’s your sponsor, how did they come to be your sponsor?

Subject:	Er it was a – my application form that I filled in, got given out to all the potential sponsors. We then had to write down our list of preference of, I think, our top 3 companies, from the list, who we would like to be sponsored by. Er, all of the companies then chose I think it was 5 or 6 students to interview – er I think I was interviewed by 4 different companies and then it was a case of the companies got in touch with the programme – I can’t remember what the technical name for him – but the guy who was gonna sort it all out, saying we’d like this student. Then he’d go round matching them up, so if 2 companies wanted the same person, then he’d give that person the first choice and I just got matched with my sponsor.

Interviewer:	Were you happy with that choice then?

Subject:	At that point in time, yes. I’ve come to realise that it was possibly not the best company I could be sponsored by, because they are a very construction based (right) company and for me now that isn’t really what I need to be doing and I can’t see myself actually managing to work on site for them. So, it’s all a bit up in the air and not necessarily the best sort of thing.

Interviewer:	Have they been very supportive of trying to find something that will fit in with you?

Subject:	I don’t know. I – I gave them a ring, but that actually before I got my exam results, in January, and said, oh, let’s see what’s going on next year. Er, and they said, oh it hasn’t been sorted out yet but have you got your exam results yet? So, obviously they wanted to know that I’d passed my exams before they did anything, but I haven’t heard back from them yet. I’m gonna ring them up. I’m just thinking how long I’m gonna leave it before I rang them up and said, er next year? But basically I explained to them that I – I would very much like to be based at home, so that I have a support network of people. I didn’t want to be taking me and my daughter, which – somewhere where I literally knew no-one – so I said to them, I ‘d really like either to go near Loughborough, so I could still have all my university friends, or near my home and that I would need regular hours. So I think it’s – I’m asking quite a lot and its basically whether they can actually, even find a job, in their company, which would suit all that or not (sighs) but I’ll have to wait and see on that one …

Interviewer:	Do you think that that is a problem for the engineering industry generally?

Subject:	I think there’s certain careers where you have to make a choice and you wouldn’t be able to be a single parent in that particular sideline of the industry. Erm, I think you could be a single parent if you were working in a design office, because you can work regular hours – 9 to 5 – and you could cope with that, but working in construction - I don’t think that’s set up at all for somebody to be looking after kids at the same time.

Interviewer:	Do you think that is because it’s so male dominated?

Subject:	It’s partly that it’s male dominated because, obviously, the general stereotypes, you know, males go off and they’ll work whatever hours they want to and the women will work their jobs round them, so they can look after the child as well or give up the job, if they can financially. Erm, and it’s partly the way the whole industry’s set up. It’s set up so that the site is open from x O’clock in the morning, through to whatever time at night. And that’s just how it has to practically be to get the jobs done, so I don’t think you’d be able to change that, no matter how much you tried.

Interviewer:	You don’t think they could be more flexible?

Subject:	I don’t – I really don’t know. I don’t think personally I’d want to go into working in construction, just purely because of the awkwardness it would cause and how I would have to say to them, yes I can work in construction, but I can only work regular hours because I have to take my daughter to nursery and pick her up. Erm, but I really don’t know. I don’t think you will manage to change the attitudes of when people are expected to work. I think it’s just you’d have to make a choice, either you work on a construction site and do the hours, or you can do the family thing. I don’t think you’d be able to change it so that you can mix both, quite effectively.

Interviewer:	Yes, so had circumstances been different, would you have been happy to stick to your…?

Subject:	Oh yeah, I’d have been perfectly happy to go and work every hour, on a construction site and I would’ve been very happy to do that. But, even if I could find child care for that length of time, I wouldn’t because that would basically mean I would never see my daughter. If you work 7 till 7 on a construction site, well, she sleeps 7 till 7, so the hours that I would be at home would be exactly when she was asleep so I definitely wouldn’t do it now but if I hadn’t had her, then yeah, I’d be perfectly happy to go and work on site all day.

Interviewer:	Er, do they expect – does your sponsor expect you to go an work for the company when you’ve finished your degree?

Subject:	Er, in general sponsored students I think it’s – some are expected and some it’s written into their contract, that they have to, whereas my particular contract, it’s just written in that I have to give serious thought to going and working for them. So, basically I’ve actually no contractual obligation, it’s just that if I am going to go and work in the construction industry, I would be expected to – the serious issue is going to work for them, but if I come out the end of the degree, decide that you know, it’s not for me, then there is no obligation or huge expectation for me to go and work for them.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the organisation?

Subject:	I tried. But you go onto their web site and it’s a mix. Some companies have an extremely small web site and it doesn’t really tell you much. It tends to highlight the projects that they’ve done and not much else about the company, so it was – it was quite difficult unless you had contacts in the industry, to find anything else out about the company apart from.

The remainder of the interview is in note format, as the recording equipment failed at this point.

Eve said that she hoped the placement would give her an opportunity to use instruments, for example in surveying. She didn’t expect group work to be a big deal, as she was used good at this anyway from doing so much team sports.

Eve felt that the best thing about going on placement would be the chance to get a feel for the industry and learning things that are impossible to learn in the classroom.
She expected the worse thing to be the long hours, giving up student life, and having less time to spend with her daughter.

She expected work to be different from being at university because you would have to act professional all the time. She also expected that she would get treated differently to being at university because of her lack of experience. She also thought the fact that she didn’t have a ‘burning desire’ to be an engineer, compared to some other students, might effect how she is treated.

In terms of career, Eve had no idea what she would be doing in the future. She had all sorts of ideas, but could only see herself in the engineering industry if she could get a 9-5 job. One of the options she is considering is doing a PGCE in Maths teaching, but she wasn’t sure whether this was a job she would like. She didn’t know what her ideal career would be, and felt like she needed help making decisions. A lot of ideas she has had, have been excluded because they don’t pay enough. Her major concern at the moment is making a decision about the placement year. She felt that she wasn’t in a position for people to help her make decisions at the moment because she literally has no idea about what to do.

While, she has enjoyed the degree, she doesn’t think she will enjoy the engineering job at the end. Although she did think that the career prospects in engineering were nothing but good, with lots of different options both in and out of the industry.

She felt that her conflict of interests were limiting her choice and career options. 

If she went through it all again, she wouldn’t get sponsorship, as now when she’s trying to make decisions she has to think about them as well as herself, and that their interests and hers were different.

She didn’t know what would happen to the money she had received from the sponsoring company, but was planning to get the advice of her personal tutor and family.

Eve described the engineering culture as intense and work-based. That it fits in with non-family oriented people, and that as an employee you are expected to be flexible to the company’s needs. Felt that family life just doesn’t fit with site work, so would have to compromise if staying in industry for office job with regular hours. Also thought that the industry was based on problem-solving.

When asked if the conflict between family and work could be resolved in the industry, she thought it would be difficult to overcome the problem because this is how site work is, and couldn’t see how else it could be organised.

End.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll tell you a little bit about what we’re doing, which is basically interviewing people, women engineering students across all different disciplines to find out, how are they going on placements and why are they going on placements and a bit about why they wanted to do engineering and their engineering experiences, so far. And we’re looking – to compare that with what it’s like when they’re in the industry (right) to get some idea of what women expect from the industry and whether the industry meets their expectations and we’re aiming to increase the retention of women in the industry (right) which is basically what we’re looking at. So if I start off asking you just a few background information questions - what course is it that you’re on?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Civil engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re doing civil engineering and is it the Master’s or the…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s – I’m undecided at the moment. I’ve got a sponsor (right) and it’s all just up in the air at the moment about whether I’m going to go or whether I’m going to stay (OK) I’m not quite certain yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What A levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did erm double maths, physics and economics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK, what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I went to a private secondary school and a state sixth form.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK. Have you got any work experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not in engineering, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are either of your parents engineers? What do they do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. My mum is something in accounts – she’s not an accountant but she does something in accounts (yeah) and my dad, he’s retired now but he was a university administrator.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so we’re going to talk about why you wanted to do engineering in the first place. So why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was basically that I was doing maths and physics at A level, and I was trying to find a degree that would have substantial proportions of that in it (yeah) and basically my physics teacher at A level was really good and I went spoke to him and said, look, these are the bits I’ve enjoyed, what do you suggest? And he suggested civil engineering and I looked into it a bit more and just…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why then did you do maths and physics A levels and not…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They were just the subjects that at GCSE I enjoyed – I was good at, and I knew I could cope with doing them at a higher level. There were other GCSE subjects that I might have enjoyed but I couldn’t see myself actually managing to complete an A level course. (yes) So, it was a combination of being good and enjoying it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about your family – were they supportive of your choices?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, they – it’s always – not been expected, but always been a highly favourable option, to go off to university and do something, like, both my older sisters did and yeah, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But the subject wasn’t really an issue?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, but I mean – I did a lot of sport when I was younger and it was – basically it was not told to me, but made sound, like, don’t do sports. So, I wasn’t really allowed to do a sport one but anything else, they were fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do any career research and did you know any – any other engineers to talk to, to speak to – what it was like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, basically, I knew that having an engineering degree wouldn’t – didn’t just lead you to doing engineering. When, I knew that if I came out with an engineering degree, I could go off and do all sorts of stuff. So to me, the fact of getting a degree was more important than the necessary career afterwards.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what does appeal to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I guess it has its logic and the mathematical bits, where in a lot of other subjects you can write an essay or write something out and it won’t necessarily have a right answer (yeah) whereas in engineering quite often, well most of the time, you work something out, you’ll come to an answer and it’s either right or wrong (yes) and I just – I like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Is there anything in particular that attracted you to civil engineering rather than say mechanical or electrical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Civil engineering just sounded more practical to me, and like it made more sense to me, so having something – and I’ve found in some modules its not quite this way, but having something you can visualise and something big like a building, you can really see it’s there, whereas things like mechanical – it all gets a bit technical.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you look into other subjects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t – I think I dismissed them quite quickly just as a kind of oh, I don’t think I’ll enjoy that bit – right, what’s next? And I came across civil and thought I’d enjoy that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to study at [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was - sport was a big pull for me and I’d had a couple of friends who’d been at [this university] – they’d had a really, really good time and I mean, in some ways, it was an added bonus that the civil engineering department happened to be really good, but it was mainly just for the sport.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you say that you’re sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was – they’ve got, in the civil engineering department, they’ve got a group of companies where you submit a general application form for sponsorship. It goes out to all those companies and then it’s – basically I didn’t see any reason not to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that after you’d started at University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was a couple of months into the first year and the department said oh, here’s the application forms – if you can fill ‘em out, fill ‘em out and give ‘em back to us and it just made sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, the indecision about the sandwich bit at the minute, is that your choice or the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That’s complicated. Er, actually in May last year, I had a baby and so it’s a case of whether I can find a job for a placement year which will allow me to still look after her because I know that if I went onto a site, I’d be expected to be on site for stupid long hours and I wouldn’t be able to look after my daughter. So it’s mostly just that if they can – if my sponsors can offer me a job where I can either be in an office, where I work regular hours, hopefully, live at home so I’ve got a support network, then I’m going into industry. If not – if they can’t offer me that then I’ll stay – just go straight on through. But that – that should be decided in the next couple of weeks.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What appeals to you about doing the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s mostly to help me have an idea of whether I actually want to go off and work in er the industry when I graduate, or whether I realise, during the year in industry, that actually it’s not for me. I’d rather realise that in one year out, than apply for a job, get a job and then realise after I’ve graduated, that actually it’s not for me. So it’s just to help me make my mind up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise it was so male-dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I knew it was quite highly male dominated, because when we went on open days around the country, like the students who’d show you round the university, from the department, would say oh yeah, there’s only 2 girls in my year and so you get to know pretty quickly. So in my maths classes and physics classes at A level, so they were male dominated and you just realise that – it’s not something that huge numbers of girls actually want to go into. So, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did that ever concern you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really, it didn’t really bother me. I mean the only – I knew that the industry was largely male dominated, and in some ways, applying to university, I thought that actually it might play in my favour, because applying as a girl, they’re trying to get girls in engineering, therefore, if on paper me and another candidate were exactly equal, the fact that I was a girl would then, perhaps – I don’t know, go in my favour and help me get on….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’ll work the same in the workplace, as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not sure because as far as the sponsorship interviews went, I got a few interviews and one in particular I went to, and another girl off my course got interviewed and she’d – both of us found that the man who was interviewing was just – didn’t want to know (right). And we almost felt like saying why did you give us an interview – if you quite blatantly – he was – I think it was partly that he just couldn’t communicate with girls, and he just found it really hard to interview us, whereas one of the guys who went for an interview, with the same man, said that they got on great, were chatting the whole way through. So that’s when you start to realise that actually it’s not a problem with the girls it’s some – I think it’s the kind of older generation of people in the industry at the moment, just struggle to see or struggle to cope with having women coming into the industry, but I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t – I’ve thought about that one quite a lot, because in some ways there’s always gonna be a finite number of girls who actually want to do a science based erm projects, and for some reason or another and I don’t know what the reason is, it’s a lower number than guys. Erm, so in some ways, encouraging girls to go into engineering might – it might get more girls doing a degree but I think the end results might not be more women going into the actual industry. It’s like I’m doing a degree but I’m not certain at the moment whether I actually want to go off and be in engineering or whether I want to go and do something else. So – er, it’s worth encouraging because there’s – there are some girls who may think, oh no, I can’t do that, boys do that. So it might get a few of them, but I don’t know how effective it would actually be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that if people aren’t so much actually encouraged into the industry that they might need to be better informed about the industry because they’ve got to make that decision? When I did A levels, I didn’t know anything about engineering so I would never even have considered it.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, that might be worth – yeah, so you would catch people who had never even considered it, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what if anything would have encouraged or discouraged you from doing engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. I don’t think – the only things that would have altered my decision, would be either my ability at the subject or my liking for it. I don’t think it has anything to do with anything on the outside of the pure subject. If there’s – I don’t really know. If there’d been more of the parts of the physics and maths that I hadn’t enjoyed, then I probably wouldn’t have done it, but because it’s full of the bits that I was good at and enjoyed, then other things really didn’t come into play that much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think ability at the subject’s got to be a foremost thing and man-management – just being able to communicate with the team, work in a team, erm, I don’t know, I guess that – I’d probably find that easier to answer if I’d actually gone out into the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any things about engineers that you would describe as male characteristics or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, even on the face of it, it’s very much the individuals that actually end up doing engineering. The girls, particularly on my course, I would say equal ability as the guys but if you take a girl from another area, who hadn’t gone into engineering, then she wouldn’t necessarily have all the qualities that she’d need. But I think, from what I’ve seen, the girls who end up doing the course I’m doing, have the attributes you need – that that’s because they’re the kind of people that will choose to do engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you’ve said that you think there may be some advantages to being a woman – do you think there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say it’s only just coming up against people in the industry who – they don’t necessarily not want women in the erm industry, but find it easier to get on with men, who apply for the job. Erm, I guess that’s one of the disadvantages. And, from personal experience, I can see how, if a woman wanted to balance family and like for example working in construction, they’d find that very difficult. I guess that’s – nowadays that’s not a disadvantage that’s purely tied to a woman. It’s just a choice that they have to make.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you started on your course here, what did you expect from your degree programme?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it what you expected in terms of like things you’ve been taught, the types of skills and gender proportions?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I mean the gender proportions actually when I arrived, there were more girls than I thought there were going to be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So I think, out of the arranged courses – there were like 28, there were 5 girls, which to me, arriving at that, seemed quite a large number. As far as what we’ve been taught, I knew that it was going to be a mix, between practical modules and management modules and that’s what’s come out of it. Some of the practical ones I didn’t foresee as us actually doing, like very much the hydraulics and fluids ones, I hadn’t really expected that so much and I think that’s shown ‘cos those are the ones I struggled more with. Those are the bits of physics I’m not very good with. But apart from that, no, it’s pretty much as I expected.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think have been the best and the worst things about your course, so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the best is, for me, coming into course without much knowledge about the whole industry, I knew the general – the general aspects, but probably just finding out more about the industry and learning about it as you, as you progress. The worst things – I don’t actually - I don’t think there are any particular aspects that I would stand like and say, oh no those have been awful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there any aspects that if you were to design the course, anything that you would change?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s ok. Have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, we’ve had one female lecturer. She’s been in the management side of it. (right) But that’s – we had one module in the first year, which was partly taught by her and a module this year, that’s been partly taught by her. Apart from that, they’re all male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are any differences in the styles of teaching between male and female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think male lecturers are a lot more – well, in general, you’ve still got exceptions, but they’re generally a lot more direct, whereas I don’t know whether it’s because of the type of module that she’s teaching – the female lecturer is more wafflely as it were (yeah) using more words and less of the mathematical and practical applications.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that male lecturers treat the female students differently to the males?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well some of them, very particularly, you see they struggle with – they’re quite happy to sit and chat to the guys but then find it very hard to – they don’t really know what to say and it’s almost as if you’re – you’re not somebody who’s normal. Er, I mean there are extreme sides of it, there’s one lecturer who – yeah – completely could not hold down a conversation with a girl if he tried, but then with other ones who’ll quite happily chat to both equally, so it’s down to individuals.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the female lecturer, did she treat all the students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, pretty much – I think so. I think it’s very interesting the way the guys on the course treat her, which perhaps makes it more difficult for her to chat to them. It’s – she’s my personal tutor so, so she knows me better anyway. So it’s quite difficult to see how she treats the other female students and the other male ones.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, yeah – I was going to ask you about personal tutors as well – are you pleased that you’ve got a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m pleased that I’ve got the personal tutor I have – particularly last year, when I was going through all the having a baby stuff, she was – she was quite good at that and I can see how some of the male personal tutors just wouldn’t have really known what to do. So I’m quite glad to have her, but I could see how actually some of the male personal tutors would have been perfectly good at it, but at the end of the day er I was quite glad to have her.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, who or what do you think has been the greatest influence on you, since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t – I don’t really know. I don’t think there has been one particular driving influence to make me – I don’t know – want to carry on and do work. It’s just – it’s a degree, its all I want at the end of the day. Well, it’s the main thing I want so I don’t think there’s been any particular influence.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever think about giving up last year then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I did think about the possibility of taking a year out but then I realised that I’d then just have a year when I was doing nothing much, erm, and at the end of the day if I’d dropped out last year, I’d have no degree, I’d have debt and basically I wouldn’t have anywhere to go. Whereas, if I stayed in University, yes, I’ll have debt by the end of it, but I’ll have a degree and actually I think I get to see my daughter a lot more being a student than I would having a proper job in the real world. So, to me, it was never particularly an option to drop out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s made you more determined in some ways?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think, because I know I have to – I really have to get this degree. I have to pass it. Whereas, before, yeah I wanted to but it wasn’t such a necessary importance – whereas now, yeah, if I – if I drop out at any point, then I’ve basically got nothing and I’ve got my daughter to support and I’ve got no way of supporting her (yeah) so everything’s a lot – well, in some ways everything’s a lot easier if I just carry on through and actually get the degree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did the type of teaching that you’ve experienced, involve much interaction with students? Like, do you have to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there’s quite a lot of the course work’s are based in a group of – of I think the biggest group’s been 6 and then all the way down to just working in pairs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you generally get to choose who you work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, last year it was mostly we were put in groups, because, obviously, you arrive at Uni and of course you don’t know anybody and it’d be difficult to – for everybody to find groups. So last year they very much put you in groups. Er, I’m sure it was done alphabetically, it was normally the same people but this year it’s much more go away, find your group (yeah), come back, tell us your group and so yeah, this year we’ve got to choose more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In that situation how do you decide who you work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh largely, people just end up working with their friends. People go with who they got on with anyway and it just makes it all a lot more simpler about trying to meet up. The – by the time we got towards the end of last year, where you were with a group of people that you just didn’t really know, didn’t get – well, didn’t not get on with, but didn’t get on with particularly well – and it is a lot easier to work in a group where it’s your friends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that males or females are easier to work with, or is that down to individuals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s just down to individuals. I’m just trying to think – I’ve worked in a few groups with one other girl in, but apart from that it’s – I’ve been working as the only girl in the group, and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really mind. Erm, I don’t think it made much difference. I don’t know whether it was the particular girl that I was working with, but it didn’t really make much difference whether it was entirely a group of guys and me, or a couple of guys with me and her (yeah). So, it didn’t end up making much difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, there was a bit of a bad exp – well, not a bad experience, but last year when they were starting to mix the groups between courses – so you’d have MENG people, BENG people and ANDN and you’d end up with all – all the ranges of abilities and levels of commitment and that was quite hard trying to get – and it ends up that I think one of the guys, who was in my group for that has – he’s since left, but I think he failed last year and it was very hard getting somebody who had a much lower level of commitment to the course, to – to work effectively in the group (Yeah). You were running around after them, hassling them to do some work but apart from that things have all just gone on quite nicely. The only problem comes when one person doesn’t do the work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. What aspects of university teaching or advice, do you think will help you if you go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, very practical based modules, like the surveying modules where you actually go out and learn how to use the instruments. I think that would be invaluable. It would be – you wouldn’t want to go onto site without that. Erm, I think the group work probably does help, in that aspect, because at least you’ve had experience before working on engineer based erm projects with a range of people and a range of skills, I guess those two things will help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any skills you’ve acquired from previous work experience might be useful on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, just working as a team, will be the only particular one from the jobs that I’ve had. Erm, being able to interact with a range or group of people who work effectively as a team.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement at the moment – this stage in the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it all depends on what job I got sent out to do. Er, I would be extremely nervous and feel slightly under prepared because a lot of people who will be going on their industrial placement worked last summer in industry, so they’ve got 3 months or whatever of experience, and I haven’t got that. I’ve never actually been onto a site but I can’t see myself ending up in a job, next year, if I do go into industry next year, that will require me to go on site all the time. I think it would be more that if I do take a placement year then it will be a placement in an office er I don’t really know what doing – design work or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the university could do anything to help students prepare more for the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There is CIVSOC, which they organise site visits and that would be very useful. Unfortunately, they go on those site visits on Wednesdays, which is when sport is, so I can’t go on those site visits. Erm, I don’t – I think the department’s set up quite well, apart from that, just to help you. There’s all sorts of people who’ve got practical experience, who you can go and talk to if you want to, er so the only thing to do to help more is to tell CIVSOC to do their visits another time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the educational experience and the way you’re taught, reflects the reality of what it’s like in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not hugely. I mean there’s a lot of stuff we’re doing now, like you’re sitting in a lecture hall, you’re writing notes and you can see how the stuff you’re being taught will help you but the – the day to day, what we do, I don’t think it’s anything like what you’d actually be doing in a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it should be geared more than it is, or do you think that they’re two separate things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s good the way it is, because if you want to get practical experience you can go off and you can get a job in your holidays or in your year out. I think that’s when you’ll find out about working on a site and all that stuff. So I think it’s – they don’t need to have any more of the practical side of it, actually on the course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, with respect to the organisation that’s your sponsor, how did they come to be your sponsor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er it was a – my application form that I filled in, got given out to all the potential sponsors. We then had to write down our list of preference of, I think, our top 3 companies, from the list, who we would like to be sponsored by. Er, all of the companies then chose I think it was 5 or 6 students to interview – er I think I was interviewed by 4 different companies and then it was a case of the companies got in touch with the programme – I can’t remember what the technical name for him – but the guy who was gonna sort it all out, saying we’d like this student. Then he’d go round matching them up, so if 2 companies wanted the same person, then he’d give that person the first choice and I just got matched with my sponsor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you happy with that choice then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At that point in time, yes. I’ve come to realise that it was possibly not the best company I could be sponsored by, because they are a very construction based (right) company and for me now that isn’t really what I need to be doing and I can’t see myself actually managing to work on site for them. So, it’s all a bit up in the air and not necessarily the best sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have they been very supportive of trying to find something that will fit in with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I – I gave them a ring, but that actually before I got my exam results, in January, and said, oh, let’s see what’s going on next year. Er, and they said, oh it hasn’t been sorted out yet but have you got your exam results yet? So, obviously they wanted to know that I’d passed my exams before they did anything, but I haven’t heard back from them yet. I’m gonna ring them up. I’m just thinking how long I’m gonna leave it before I rang them up and said, er next year? But basically I explained to them that I – I would very much like to be based at home, so that I have a support network of people. I didn’t want to be taking me and my daughter, which – somewhere where I literally knew no-one – so I said to them, I ‘d really like either to go near Loughborough, so I could still have all my university friends, or near my home and that I would need regular hours. So I think it’s – I’m asking quite a lot and its basically whether they can actually, even find a job, in their company, which would suit all that or not (sighs) but I’ll have to wait and see on that one …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that that is a problem for the engineering industry generally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there’s certain careers where you have to make a choice and you wouldn’t be able to be a single parent in that particular sideline of the industry. Erm, I think you could be a single parent if you were working in a design office, because you can work regular hours – 9 to 5 – and you could cope with that, but working in construction - I don’t think that’s set up at all for somebody to be looking after kids at the same time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is because it’s so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s partly that it’s male dominated because, obviously, the general stereotypes, you know, males go off and they’ll work whatever hours they want to and the women will work their jobs round them, so they can look after the child as well or give up the job, if they can financially. Erm, and it’s partly the way the whole industry’s set up. It’s set up so that the site is open from x O’clock in the morning, through to whatever time at night. And that’s just how it has to practically be to get the jobs done, so I don’t think you’d be able to change that, no matter how much you tried.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You don’t think they could be more flexible?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t – I really don’t know. I don’t think personally I’d want to go into working in construction, just purely because of the awkwardness it would cause and how I would have to say to them, yes I can work in construction, but I can only work regular hours because I have to take my daughter to nursery and pick her up. Erm, but I really don’t know. I don’t think you will manage to change the attitudes of when people are expected to work. I think it’s just you’d have to make a choice, either you work on a construction site and do the hours, or you can do the family thing. I don’t think you’d be able to change it so that you can mix both, quite effectively.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, so had circumstances been different, would you have been happy to stick to your…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, I’d have been perfectly happy to go and work every hour, on a construction site and I would’ve been very happy to do that. But, even if I could find child care for that length of time, I wouldn’t because that would basically mean I would never see my daughter. If you work 7 till 7 on a construction site, well, she sleeps 7 till 7, so the hours that I would be at home would be exactly when she was asleep so I definitely wouldn’t do it now but if I hadn’t had her, then yeah, I’d be perfectly happy to go and work on site all day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Er, do they expect – does your sponsor expect you to go an work for the company when you’ve finished your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, in general sponsored students I think it’s – some are expected and some it’s written into their contract, that they have to, whereas my particular contract, it’s just written in that I have to give serious thought to going and working for them. So, basically I’ve actually no contractual obligation, it’s just that if I am going to go and work in the construction industry, I would be expected to – the serious issue is going to work for them, but if I come out the end of the degree, decide that you know, it’s not for me, then there is no obligation or huge expectation for me to go and work for them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into the organisation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I tried. But you go onto their web site and it’s a mix. Some companies have an extremely small web site and it doesn’t really tell you much. It tends to highlight the projects that they’ve done and not much else about the company, so it was – it was quite difficult unless you had contacts in the industry, to find anything else out about the company apart from. The remainder of the interview is in note format, as the recording equipment failed at this point. Eve said that she hoped the placement would give her an opportunity to use instruments, for example in surveying. She didn’t expect group work to be a big deal, as she was used good at this anyway from doing so much team sports. Eve felt that the best thing about going on placement would be the chance to get a feel for the industry and learning things that are impossible to learn in the classroom. She expected the worse thing to be the long hours, giving up student life, and having less time to spend with her daughter. She expected work to be different from being at university because you would have to act professional all the time. She also expected that she would get treated differently to being at university because of her lack of experience. She also thought the fact that she didn’t have a ‘burning desire’ to be an engineer, compared to some other students, might effect how she is treated. In terms of career, Eve had no idea what she would be doing in the future. She had all sorts of ideas, but could only see herself in the engineering industry if she could get a 9-5 job. One of the options she is considering is doing a PGCE in Maths teaching, but she wasn’t sure whether this was a job she would like. She didn’t know what her ideal career would be, and felt like she needed help making decisions. A lot of ideas she has had, have been excluded because they don’t pay enough. Her major concern at the moment is making a decision about the placement year. She felt that she wasn’t in a position for people to help her make decisions at the moment because she literally has no idea about what to do. While, she has enjoyed the degree, she doesn’t think she will enjoy the engineering job at the end. Although she did think that the career prospects in engineering were nothing but good, with lots of different options both in and out of the industry. She felt that her conflict of interests were limiting her choice and career options. If she went through it all again, she wouldn’t get sponsorship, as now when she’s trying to make decisions she has to think about them as well as herself, and that their interests and hers were different. She didn’t know what would happen to the money she had received from the sponsoring company, but was planning to get the advice of her personal tutor and family. Eve described the engineering culture as intense and work-based. That it fits in with non-family oriented people, and that as an employee you are expected to be flexible to the company’s needs. Felt that family life just doesn’t fit with site work, so would have to compromise if staying in industry for office job with regular hours. Also thought that the industry was based on problem-solving. When asked if the conflict between family and work could be resolved in the industry, she thought it would be difficult to overcome the problem because this is how site work is, and couldn’t see how else it could be organised. End.
